{{short description|On distance between centers of a triangle}}
[[File:Euler theorem2.svg|thumb|right|upright=1.0|Euler's theorem:<br/><math>d=|IO| =\sqrt{R (R-2r)}</math>]]
In [[geometry]], '''Euler's theorem''' states that the distance ''d'' between the [[circumcenter]] and [[incenter]] of a [[triangle]] is given by{{r|Johnson|Dunham}}
<math display=block> d^2=R (R-2r) </math>
or equivalently
<math display=block> \frac{1}{R-d} + \frac{1}{R+d} = \frac{1}{r},</math>
where <math>R</math> and <math>r</math> denote the circumradius and inradius respectively (the radii of the [[circumscribed circle]] and [[inscribed circle]] respectively). The theorem is named for  [[Leonhard Euler]], who published it in 1765.{{r|LevershaSmith}} However, the same result was published earlier by [[William Chapple (surveyor)|William Chapple]] in 1746.{{r|Chapple}}

From the theorem follows the '''Euler inequality''':{{r|wlim}}
<math display=block> R \ge 2r,</math>
which holds with equality only in the [[equilateral triangle|equilateral]] case.{{r|SV}}

== Proof ==
{{unsourced section|date=June 2026}}
[[File:Вики _.png|thumb|Proof of Euler's theorem]]

Let <math>O</math> be the center of the circumcircle of triangle <math>ABC</math>, and let <math>I</math> be the center of its incircle.

If the ray <math>AI</math> intersects the circumcircle at the point <math>L</math>, then <math>L</math> is the midpoint of arc <math>BC</math>. Draw the ray <math>LO</math> and denote its intersection with the circumcircle by <math>M</math>.

Then <math>LM</math> is a diameter of the circumcircle. Drop the perpendicular <math>ID</math> from the point <math>I</math> to <math>AB</math>. Then <math>ID = r</math>. Rewrite Euler's formula in the following form:

: <math>d^2 - R^2 = -2rR</math>

Notice that the left-hand side is the [[Power of a point|power]] of the point <math>I</math> with respect to the circumcircle.

Therefore, it suffices to prove the equality <math>LI \cdot IA = 2Rr</math>.

By the [[Incenter–excenter lemma|trident lemma]], <math>LI = LB,</math> so it suffices to prove that <math>LB \cdot IA = 2Rr</math>.

Now observe that <math>2R = LM</math> and <math>r = ID,</math> that is, the required equality can be rewritten as <math>LB \cdot IA = LM \cdot ID.</math> Rewriting it once more, we obtain <math>LB / LM = ID / IA</math>.

This equality follows from the [[Similarity (geometry)|similarity]] of triangles <math>\triangle AID</math> and <math>\triangle MLB</math>.

Indeed, the angles at <math>B</math> and <math>D</math> in these triangles are right angles, while the angles at <math>A</math> and <math>M</math> are equal because they both [[Inscribed angle|subtend]] the arc <math>BL</math> (moreover, the ratio <math>LB / LM = ID / IA</math> is equal to the [[Sine|sine]] of the angle <math>\angle BAL</math>).

==Stronger version of the inequality==
A stronger version{{r|SV}} is
<math display=block>\frac{R}{r} \geq \frac{abc+a^3+b^3+c^3}{2abc} \geq \frac{a}{b}+\frac{b}{c}+\frac{c}{a}-1 \geq \frac{2}{3} \left(\frac{a}{b}+\frac{b}{c}+\frac{c}{a} \right) \geq 2,</math>
where <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, and <math>c</math> are the side lengths of the triangle.

==Euler's theorem for the escribed circle==
If <math>r_a</math> and <math>d_a</math> denote respectively the radius of the [[escribed circle]] opposite to the vertex <math>A</math> and the distance between its center and the center of 
the circumscribed circle, then <math>d_a^2=R(R+2r_a)</math>.

==Euler's inequality in absolute geometry==
Euler's inequality, in the form stating that, for all triangles inscribed in a given circle, the maximum of the radius of the inscribed circle is reached for the equilateral triangle and only for it, is valid in [[absolute geometry]].{{r|PS}}

==See also==
*[[Bicentric quadrilateral#Fuss' theorem|Fuss' theorem]] for the relation among the same three variables in bicentric quadrilaterals
*[[Poncelet's closure theorem]], showing that there is an infinity of triangles with the same two circles (and therefore the same ''R'', ''r'', and ''d'')
*[[Egan conjecture]], generalization to higher dimensions
*[[List of triangle inequalities]]
